problem: Prior VLN-CE agents either depend on panoramic RGB-D, odometry and simulator-pretrained waypoint predictors that transfer poorly to real robots, or, as with end-to-end VLAs, map language directly to quantized low-level commands. No prior system carried language instructions all the way to leg-joint control on legged robots navigating cluttered real scenes. Existing VLN-CE benchmarks in Habitat also ignore physical execution; for example, agents can pass through 10 cm gaps.
motivation: Legged robots can traverse cluttered and rough terrain that wheeled robots cannot, and language is a flexible interface for commanding them. VLMs are trained on natural language, so forcing them to emit precise non-verbal low-level actions wastes their reasoning ability. Recent VLMs, however, show good spatial and distance reasoning in language (SpatialVLM, SpatialRGPT). That suggests expressing actions as mid-level language such as 'move forward 75cm' and handing execution to a robust RL locomotion policy.
key_idea: Fine-tune an image-based VLM (VILA-8B) on single-view RGB video to output mid-level navigation actions in natural language (direction plus metric distance or angle), and execute them with a separately trained, LiDAR-heightmap-based single-stage RL locomotion policy. This decouples reasoning from embodiment-specific control.
insight: Keeping both input and output in the language domain lets the VLA train on heterogeneous data: human YouTube touring videos, ScanQA, and general VQA. It can also be reused across robots (Go2, H1, T1) without retraining. Ablations point to data and execution rather than architecture as the main levers: (1) Human touring videos raise R2R-CE SR from 49.7 to 54.0 and real-world Go2 Outdoor SR from 0.00 to 1.00. (2) Label rebalancing is critical: without it, R2R-CE SR drops from 49.7 to 30.0. (3) RxR data adds little to R2R-CE (47.7 without RxR vs 49.7 with). (4) 8 history frames are nearly as good as 64 (49.7 vs 50.1 SR). (5) In the physics-realistic VLN-CE-Isaac benchmark, the LiDAR vision locomotion policy almost closes the gap to perfect command execution (Go2 SR 50.2 vs oracle 51.3), whereas a blind policy loses about 15 SR (Go2) and about 27 SR (H1). Low-level obstacle avoidance therefore compensates for VLA mistakes.
method: Image-based VLA on VILA: starts from the VILA stage-2 checkpoint (8B, vision encoder + MLP projector + LLM); all modules are unfrozen and fine-tuned for one epoch on the SFT blend (lr 1e-4, cosine decay, warm-up 0.03).

Navigation prompt / frame sampling: the latest frame is kept as the current observation and the previous t-1 frames are uniformly sampled as memory, always including the first frame (8-64 frames). The two are distinguished only by textual cues ('a video of historical observations:' / 'current observation:'), with no special tokens.

Mid-level language actions: the VLA outputs forward/turn-left/turn-right/stop with metric arguments, e.g. 'turn right 30 degrees'. A regex parser extracts action type and value. Training labels merge up to 3 consecutive oracle Habitat steps (25 cm / 15°) to create continuous-valued distances and angles, and stop labels are rebalanced.

Human-video data pipeline: 2K YouTube egocentric touring videos are turned into 20K trajectories via entropy-based sampling. Step-wise actions come from MASt3R metric camera poses, and instructions from VILA captioning plus GPT-4o rephrasing. Used directly as continuous navigation training data.

SFT blend: R2R-CE and RxR-CE shortest-path step-wise videos from Habitat, EnvDrop augmented instructions, an auxiliary trajectory-summarization task (video to instruction), ScanQA multi-view 3D QA, and general VQA (LLaVA-1.5, ShareGPT4V, Video-ChatGPT).

Single-stage visual locomotion RL: PPO in Isaac Lab (>60K FPS on an RTX 4090) with an asymmetric actor-critic. The critic gets privileged terrain height scan and linear velocity; the actor gets proprioception history plus a 2.5D height map built from Unitree L1 LiDAR (min per voxel, max filter over 5 scans). Outputs 12 desired joint positions. No teacher-student distillation. VLA commands map to 0.5 m/s or ±π/6 rad/s for a matching duration.

VLN-CE-Isaac benchmark: R2R val-unseen scenes ported to Isaac Sim with physically simulated robots (Go2, H1). Keeps 1,077 of 1,839 traversable, high-quality-mesh trajectories, so evaluation covers the full stack from planning to joint control.

setting.backbone: NaVILA-8B: VILA-8B VLM (fully fine-tuned) for high-level mid-level language actions + PPO-trained MLP locomotion policy (LiDAR height map + proprioception) for joint control
setting.training_data: R2R-CE + RxR-CE step-wise shortest-path videos from Habitat (merged actions, rebalanced stop labels); EnvDrop augmented instructions + trajectory summarization; ScanQA multi-view QA; 20K trajectories from 2K YouTube human touring videos (MASt3R poses, VILA+GPT-4o instructions); general VQA (LLaVA-1.5, ShareGPT4V, Video-ChatGPT). Locomotion policy trained with PPO in Isaac Lab on flat, rough, slope and obstacle terrains with domain randomization.
setting.observation: VLA: monocular single-view RGB (current frame + uniformly sampled history, 8-64 frames; 8 in real world); no depth, panorama or odometry. Locomotion: proprioception history + 2.5D height map from 360° LiDAR (Go2) / height scan (H1 in sim).
setting.action_space: Mid-level language actions (move forward X cm, turn left/right X degrees, stop), parsed by regex. On the robot these become velocity commands (0.5 m/s, ±π/6 rad/s) held for the matching duration, then 12-DoF desired joint positions from the RL policy. In Habitat VLN-CE they are executed as continuous forward/turn moves.
setting.simulator: Habitat (VLN-CE R2R/RxR); Isaac Sim / Isaac Lab (VLN-CE-Isaac, locomotion training)
setting.privileged: none at test time (privileged terrain heights used only by the RL critic during training)

results: With single-view RGB only, NaVILA reaches 54.0 SR / 49.0 SPL on R2R-CE val-unseen and 49.3 SR / 44.0 SPL / 58.8 nDTW on RxR-CE val-unseen. This far exceeds the previous single-view SOTA NaVid (37.0 SR on R2R-CE, the '17%' gain) and all methods without waypoint predictors, and is comparable to panoramic RGB-D waypoint methods such as ETPNav (57.0), though below HNR (61.0) and BEVBert (59.0). In cross-dataset transfer to RxR-CE it reaches 34.3 SR vs NaVid's 23.8, and on ScanQA it reaches 102.7 CIDEr vs NaviLLM's 75.9. The single-stage locomotion policy cuts collision rate to 0.81 vs 3.09 for ROA. On VLN-CE-Isaac, the vision policy beats the blind one by 14 SR on Go2 (50.2 vs 36.2) and 21 SR on H1 (45.3 vs 24.4). Real-world Go2/T1 deployment clearly beats GPT-4o, e.g. Home-complex SR 0.67 vs 0.00.
limitations: Cannot recover from deviations: real-world failures occur when the robot drifts off course, e.g. never reaching the bedroom. There is no explicit error-correction or reasoning mechanism.
The 8B image-based VLM is computationally heavy: about 1 FPS on an RTX 4090 and run off-board, so images must be transmitted. Quantization helps but on-robot deployment is left as future work.

Still behind panoramic RGB-D waypoint-predictor methods (HNR, BEVBert, ETPNav) on R2R-CE. The real-world evaluation is small (25 instructions × 3 trials), and VLN-CE-Isaac uses only 1,077 of 1,839 val-unseen episodes.
